subject: chopperMotorbike
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: custom chopper motorbike.
Style: Overwatch.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module for an Overwatch-style chopper motorbike, with bold stylized shapes and glowing accents, structuring it around a root frame joint plus wheels, fork, and handlebar joints, and now sketching out the overall dimensions.

For the wheels I'm working out how to build them using lathe geometry around the X axis, defining a tire profile with inner and outer radius points to form a chunky tire silhouette, plus a separate rim, hub, and spoke structure with a bright cyan glowing accent ring to fit the stylized Overwatch palette.

I'm settling on a navy frame, orange tank, cyan glow, cream stripes, and chrome grey, with a generic circular emblem decal on the tank instead of a trademarked logo. Now I'm sketching out the joint skeleton — a root frame, a swingarm pivoting to the rear wheel, and a raked steering head angling forward and down for that chopper-style stance.

Working through the fork geometry to find the right axle position for a 0.34 radius front wheel, placing the steering head at roughly [0, 0.98, 0.35] and solving for an axle around [0, 0.34, 0.85] so the fork length and angle look like extended telescoping forks.

Now I'm laying out the remaining joints: a handlebar joint at the head, wheelF at the front axle, and a rear axle around [0, 0.36, -1.05] for a fatter 0.38-radius rear tire, making sure wheel centers sit at their radius height so the tires touch the floor properly. I'm deciding to keep the joint set minimal -- frame, fork, bars, wheelF, swing, wheelR -- skipping extras like kickstand and footpegs for now since this isn't a creature rig needing those roles.

I'm sketching the chopper's hardtail frame geometry: a raked steering head tube, a backbone running from the head down through the seat post to the rear, and rod/capsule construction for left-right mirrored tubes using chrome and dark coloring.

Now I'm laying out the down tube from the head to the engine mount, the lower rail toward the rear axle, and the seat stays connecting to the axle region, positioning everything relative to the tire's half-width so the stays clear it, before moving on to the V-twin engine block.

Building the crankcase box with dark metal and orange accents, then angling the two cylinders forward and back along the z-plane with a lathed fin profile for each...

Writing cylinder fin outlines...

I'll add glowing cyan power-core discs on the crankcase sides for an Overwatch-style tech look, plus chrome exhaust pipes sweeping from the cylinders down and back with flared cyan-accented tips using catmull curves.

Now I'm shaping the dual exhaust pipes with tapered radii and flared ends, then sculpting the fuel tank as a teardrop loft with a custom radius profile and orange/cream countershade paint stripes.

Working out decal placement...

I'll use the surface's around/at method with azimuth 90 for +X elevation 0, handling a null hit by skipping, and pass the hit directly since it sets direction to its normal.

For the emblem design, I'm keeping it symmetric since mirroring across the flank is tricky, and confirming SVG decals support alpha. For the seat, I'm planning to extrude a side-profile outline (a solo bobber-style saddle) with thickness along the appropriate axis to get a centered seat shape.

Rather than a constant-width extrude, I think a loft with varying station widths makes more sense for the tapered seat — narrow at the nose, widening toward the back, with a slight rear lift, colored brown leather with orange piping stitch detail. Now I'm thinking through ape hanger handlebars with a swept shape.

Still mapping handlebar curve... I'll add orange grips, mirrored mirrors with cyan lenses, small brake levers, and position everything as children of the fork/handlebar joint.

For the headlight I'm giving it a dark bucket shape with a glowing cyan-white lens, Tracer-style. Then I'm setting up the wheels—skinny front tire (~0.07 half-width), fat rear (~0.15), with lathe-built rims and a thin cyan accent ring on each sidewall for that exaggerated Overwatch chunkiness.

Still writing wheel geometry...

Working out the box placement...

Now I'm thinking about the ring line as the wheel's axis — the joint's bone direction should align with the wheel's rotation axis so spokes spin correctly with the wheel. I need to make sure the wheel joint's aim direction is set along the sideways axis, and trace through how the fork joint connects to the wheel joint in the chain.

For the spokes, I'm working out the orientation: since the ring item's local Z axis points along the wheel's axial direction, the spoke's box geometry needs to be sized so its thickness sits correctly along that axial direction while extending outward as the radial spoke.

I'm thinking about adding six spokes per side for a tech-styled mag wheel look, plus a cyan-glowing hub cap at the axle to tie in the accent color. For the rear tire, I'm considering whether to add tread detailing or painted stripe accents, though that might be optional polish.

Writing tread pattern logic...

Now I'm thinking through the rear fender as an arc sweep around the rear axle, choosing a center point and start angle so the flattened elliptical strip curves correctly over the wheel.

I'm going with a hardtail design, rigid frame mount for the rear fender in chunky orange with a cream edge, plus a small red-orange taillight lens. For the front, I'll add a minimal arc fender over the front wheel mounted to the fork for extra character.

Working through fender-fork geometry...

Working out the triple tree geometry now, computing fork top positions from the head tube and verifying the stanchion lines connect correctly to the axle points using the direction vector math.

Positioning the lower tree and head tube geometry, then placing the headlight bucket in front of the triple trees between the fork legs.

Writing lathe profile for the headlight shell and lens, with an orange bucket and cyan-tinted lens dome...

Now I'm working out the chrome rim ring and the fork support rods connecting the headlight brackets to the legs, plus the engine crankcase box and cylinder blocks with a dark metal finish, adding a lathe-based primary cover disc on the side.

Defining the lathe profiles for the power core glow rings and the orange crankcase shell, then setting up angled cylinder directions for the front and rear engine cylinders with fin lathes and cylinder head boxes on top.

I'm now placing the head covers with cyan and orange accents and rocker-box details, plus adding the chrome air cleaner intake on the right side as a lathe cone with a cyan ring.

I'm positioning cylinders and heads front-to-back along the z-axis, with the air cleaner tucked in between so it clears both the cylinders and the fuel tank sitting above.

Working out the frame cradle geometry, placing the down tubes and rails relative to the crankcase so they pass outside it cleanly, defining the tube path points from the head down through the cradle split.

Now I'm routing the lower stays to the rear axle plates and the upper seat stays back from the backbone, plus a seat post rod connecting backbone to the cradle, closing the frame structure. I'm also settling on a dark steel charcoal frame with orange and cyan accents plus cream and chrome details to match the Overwatch palette.

I'm adding the axle plates with cyan nut rings and a chrome axle rod through the wheel, and I'm sketching a curved sissy bar behind the seat with a cushioned pad for the backrest.

Now I'm placing forward foot controls—chrome pegs with orange tips mounted horizontally near the front wheel, connected back to the frame rails with a support rod.

I'll skip a kickstand since the wheels already contact the floor, and add a gas cap on the tank top, a small chrome cylinder ringed in cyan, positioned by casting a ray down onto the tank surface.

A speedometer gauge gets placed on the handlebar mid-section as a tilted cylinder with a cyan glass face aimed toward the rider, and I'm now routing dual exhaust pipes back from the cylinder ports along each side of the frame.

I'm checking pipe placement against the pegs and rear wheel clearance, positioning the pipes outside the pegs at a raised height so they clear the wheel stays, then adding heat shield bands partway along their length using wider sweep segments.

Now I'm designing a flared chrome exhaust tip at the pipe's end using a lathe shape, working out a non-self-crossing outline for the cone mouth and orienting it along the pipe's tangent direction so the flare sits naturally at the terminus.

I'm considering adding a small cyan disc inside the tip for a glowing tailpipe effect, then moving on to work out the seat placement sitting atop the backbone frame, lofting its profile at the right height and width to position it correctly behind the fender and fork.

I'm also checking how the fuel tank mounts against the backbone, making sure its bottom curve meets the frame's height at that point and sweeping its centerline accordingly.

Now I need the tank's front edge to clear the head tube and handlebar riser, so I'm shrinking its length and rounding the front taper so it ends before colliding with the steering components.

Calculating the tank's radius profile...

Working out the tiger-stripe paint logic...

I'll use sectors for the tank, keeping it robust without extra paint logic. For the decal, I'm planning a circular emblem with a cream ring, navy inner circle, and orange chevron, placed on each flank via a surface decal anchored around the tank center at azimuth 90 for the left side, skipping mirroring for now since the orientation should read correctly as-is.

For the emblem itself, I'm sketching an SVG with a dark circle outlined in cream, an orange upward chevron arrow, and maybe a small accent shape — skipping extra decals like a rear plate for simplicity. I still need to handle the wheel hub as a lathed cyan piece and make sure the tire geometry actually touches the ground plane at y=0, checking whether the revolve segmentation puts a vertex exactly at the bottom.

I'm nudging the wheel radius and axle height down slightly (a few millimeters) so the tire sinks just enough into the floor rather than hovering, then deriving the fork and head tube positions from that adjusted front axle height.

Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy: a root frame joint, a fork joint parented to the head with its aim toward the front axle, a handlebar joint above that, and front/rear wheel joints parented appropriately with their rotation axis along X. I'm also considering whether to add a kickstand joint for extra detail.

For the handlebars, I'm shaping an ape-hanger style curve using a series of 3D points that sweep upward and back, mirrored for each side, then rendering it as a chrome tube with a catmull-rom path and small sweep radius.

I'm giving the grip area a thicker dark-orange sweep radius for the last section of the handlebar path, then considering whether to skip adding brake levers and mirror stalks since they're adding too much complexity.

Actually, I'll add small rounded chrome mirrors on each side — a short rod rising from the grip base to a flat disc-shaped mirror head with a cyan lens inset, aiming outward. For the rear, I'm placing a small orange-red taillight box near the fender end to match the Overwatch-style palette.

A small white license plate at the back could work too, maybe with a simple numeric decal like "76" using basic shapes rather than text rendering to avoid font issues. I also need to add the belt/chain drive linking the engine sprocket to the rear wheel sprocket using rod segments and a lathe-disc sprocket near the rear wheel hub.

I need to reconsider the engine case position since it conflicts with the pulley placement -- maybe put the power core on both sides symmetrically and shift the belt outside it, leaving room for the pipe further out.

Simplifying: I'll place small cores on both sides of the crankcase at a fixed radius, and route the belt from the transmission behind the engine block instead, so it doesn't collide with the core discs.

I'm also sketching a thin cyan underglow slab beneath the crankcase for an Overwatch-style light bar effect, matching the tank's cyan accent.

Now I'm adding small hero-tech tail fins at the rear fender—orange with cyan edges, extruded as vertical shark-fin shapes off the fender's back end.

Shifting to checking fender and seat geometry for overlap, I'm recalculating where the fender top curve meets the seat's rear edge in z and y coordinates to make sure they align without clipping.

I'm then adjusting the fender's angular sweep from the top point, testing different arc extents (from 30° forward to varying degrees backward) to get a reasonable overall bike length while leaving room for a taillight at the rear end of the fender.

Now I'm setting up the wheels using lathe shapes mounted on axle bones with the rotation axis along x, then working out the rim geometry as a separate hoop profile sunk slightly into the tire's inner radius so the sidewalls read correctly.

Writing wheel geometry function...

Still defining the lathe geometry...

I'll generate the spoke ring directly at the wheel joint using its axis as the bone, with the joint itself created from the fork and axle position. Rim can stay a simple disc for now, and I'm jotting down the color palette (orange, dark orange, navy) to use for the model.

Now I'm setting up vector and point helper functions, then starting the actual build script with imports and builder setup.

Still defining the fork, handlebar, and wheel joints...

I'm debating whether to add a kickstand joint too, but it seems overly fussy for a folded pose, so I'll just skip it and keep the existing joint set.

For the frame geometry, I decide to use capsules instead of flat-ended rods so joints look seamless where tubes meet, bound to the frame bone. Now I'm building the backbone sweep using a catmull-rom path through a series of points.

Still working out down tube...

Adding axle rod and nut details...

Now I'm setting up the engine with a crankcase box centered at the crank position, attaching it to the frame joint and adding an orange cap on top.

I'm refining the crankcase shape, adding an orange belt band around it, a transmission box behind, and lathe-profile ring cores for the engine sides.

Still working out the cylinder placements for the V-angle and generating the fin outline geometry as a repeating zigzag pattern...

Now I'm blocking in the engine head shape with an orange box and a navy rocker cover on top, positioned along the cylinder direction.

I'm positioning an air cleaner near the overlapping cylinder bases with a small lathe-dish shape and chrome cap, then deciding to skip the carb-to-cylinder connector since it would be hidden. Now I'm working out the exhaust port geometry on the front cylinder head, starting the path from a point near the head's side.

Checking the head height against the tank bottom, I find the cylinder tops poke slightly into the tank sweep, but since that's a hidden region it's acceptable; still, I consider lowering the crank or shortening the fin count to clean up the geometry.

Settling on 5 fins with adjusted spacing, I work out the head and cover heights so they clear the tank properly, then start plotting the exhaust pipe path curving outward and downward from the side of the head toward the frame.

I'm simplifying to one exhaust pipe per side rather than stacking multiple pipes per cylinder, keeping the geometry symmetric and cleaner-looking.

For a heat shield, I'm adding a slightly larger-radius sweep segment over part of the pipe using the same radius function plus a small offset, colored dark navy instead of orange or chrome to fit the overall palette.

Then I'm lathing a flared pipe end backward along the z-axis, with an optional small cyan ring disc near the opening, matching the tangent direction from the pipe's path curve. After that I'm moving on to build out the tank, seat, fenders, headlight, bars, fork, wheels, decals, sissy bar, plate, fin, and taillight, starting with an orange tank featuring sectioned color panels.

For the tank, I'm sweeping a teardrop-shaped cross-section along the tank path, defining the radius function so it's taller than wide with a front-heavy peak, and attaching it only to the frame bone. Then I'm adding a chrome gas cap with a small cyan ring embedded into the tank surface via a raycast hit point.

Now I'm moving to the seat, lofting through a series of cross-sections along the frame to shape it wider in the middle and narrower at the front and back, and thinking about whether to add piping or rivet details along the edges for extra detail.

Checking the backbone curve at that depth, it passes right through the seat bottom, so I should raise the seat higher to clear it, even if that makes the seat height unrealistically tall for a chopper.

Working out the seat post, upper stay, and rear fender placement relative to the backbone, then starting on the sissy bar's curved path using a spline through several points above the seat.

Still adjusting sissy bar positions...

I'm positioning a small plate and tail light near the fender's rear end, angling the plate to match the fender's outward-facing normal and placing a red sphere light just above it, then starting an SVG for the plate texture.

Still writing SVG code...

I'm checking the fender arc clearance against the headlight position, then working out the lathe profile coordinates for the headlight bucket shape, defining its outline points as a cross-section to be revolved around the vertical axis.

Now I'm adding the chrome ring and lens details for the headlight, refining the radial coordinates so the ring and lens fit cleanly against the bucket's rim, then starting to plan the mounting rods connecting the fork legs to the headlight sides.

Still placing fork components...

Mapping out the bar curve as a catmull-rom sweep rising from the stem up into ape-hanger style tips that curl back toward the rider, with the grip radius tapering near the ends and flat round caps.

Now figuring out the mirror placement: taking a point along the bar path, building a capsule outward and up to form the mirror stem, then attaching a cylindrical mirror head angled outward and back at the top.

Positioning the mirror glass slightly offset toward the rider on the -z side, then placing a speedometer gauge on the top of the triple tree with a steel body and a cyan face disc offset forward.

Now I'm working out the front fender geometry — computing its arc from the front axle using a radius matching the wheel, spanning roughly from 35° in front to 25° behind top dead center, and verifying the rotation direction around the -X axis maps Y toward -Z correctly for the arc's handedness.

I'm sweeping the fender shape along this path with a flat elliptical cross-section (wide and thin) colored orange, then painting a navy stripe sector along the top of the tube.

Now working out the rear fender geometry: placing its center relative to the rear axle at a 30° forward angle with radius 0.415, sweeping a 90° arc, and sizing its half-width to 0.17 so it clears the 0.38-radius tire with a comfortable gap.

For the taillight, I'm computing where that 90° arc ends—60° behind top—to position a scaled sphere there for the light, plus a license plate just below it.

Then I'm adding the underglow and skid plate pieces: a thin cyan strip and a steel skid plate sitting at crankcase level, and starting to work out the footpeg mounting points along the rail.

Positioning pegs, pipes, and checking clearances...

I'm alternating tread block colors around the tire using paint based on angle, and considering adding a brake rotor disc on the front wheel as a decorative lathe shape.

Still positioning rotor geometry...

Settling on rotor as a flat ring from radius .05–.17 so it touches the hub cylinder cleanly at the inner edge, keeping it simple rather than adding cutout detail. For the rear wheel, since it uses a belt sprocket instead of a disc rotor, I'm sizing a similar hub lathe shape with its own radius and length to fit the rear tire's wider profile.

Now I'm placing the belt drive: a transmission pulley near the frame and belt rods running from it back to the rear sprocket, but I need to shift the belt's x-position outward so it clears the rear stay and axle plates without overlapping them.

Actually, every placement conflicts with the stays, so I'm abandoning the belt and sprocket idea entirely — no chain drive, just a plain axle on the rear left. I considered adding a brake rotor on the rear right instead, but that hits the same stay conflict, so I'm skipping it too.

Part count still looks manageable, under a thousand. Now I'm sizing the rear tire — width, radius, rim radius, and inner radius — and working out the spoke lengths for the rim hoop.

Spoke length... working that out...

Now I'm figuring out the spoke geometry for the fat rear wheel, deciding the axial slab width so the rim face stays visible, and setting the box dimensions for tangential, radial, and axial directions, matching the front wheel proportions too. I'm also working through the spoke orientation logic, aligning the local box axes to the wheel joint axis so the spokes point correctly toward the hub.

To reduce the risk of misaligned orientation, I'm switching from boxes to tapered cylindrical pillars for the spokes since they're rotationally symmetric and give a chunky mechanical look regardless of axis assumptions. I'm starting to write the wheel function now, defining the rim hoop, cyan ring accents, and hub lathe geometry along the axle.

Deciding on chrome rims with steel/navy spokes and a cyan hub cap for contrast. Writing rim lathe geometry...

Setting hub height relative to the half-width, then designing tapered end caps and a ring of six spokes connecting into the hub geometry.

I'm second-guessing whether the embed parameter assumes a centered or base-aligned cylinder — I may need to translate the geometry so its base sits at the origin to avoid an unintended offset along the axis.

Translation should work fine either way, so I'll go with that approach. Now I'm working out the rotor placement for the front wheel lathe, positioning it along the axle offset from the hub so it clears the fork leg and hub cap without collision, checking that all the x-coordinates for rotor, hub, and cap stay within the fork leg boundary.

For the rear wheel I realize the hub cap ends up recessed inside the tire's sidewall, hidden from view, so I'm adjusting the hub height to equal the wheel width so the caps extend out properly—front hub to .07, rear to .15—and extending the axle rod to pass through both sides. I also need to double check the front rotor position relative to the hub end so they don't overlap.

Checking the rotor geometry again, I confirm its inner radius of .04 sits in empty space between the hub and tire sidewall, clear of the thin radial spoke cylinders which only extend to about .028 in that direction, so no collision there. I'll move on to thinking about adding decals next.

Deciding to skip the headlight emblem and focus on the gas tank decal placement instead, I compute the tank's surface geometry: locating the flank point where the tank radius peaks around .15, giving a surface z-coordinate near .04 for centering a .13x.13 decal, oriented along the tank's curve using the surface-wrap helper to find the hit point and direction.

But I then notice a collision — the tank's rear curves down into the seat's nose, overlapping where the seat top meets the tank bottom near z=-.05. To fix this, I'm shortening the tank path and shifting the seat nose further back to z=-.28 or so, re-adjusting the station widths and heights to avoid the overlap.

Checking the gap between the backbone frame and tank bottom near z=.05, there's about a .07 gap — I'm considering adding a small strap or support rod connecting the backbone to the tank to mount it properly.

Next I'm sorting out the backbone points near the front, tank floor radius to avoid degenerate ends, and finishing up the seat/backrest pad detail before moving on to the taillight.

Thinking about bold Overwatch-style accents now: adding cyan ring clamps along the pipes using path frames so each ring orients with the pipe's tangent, plus possibly cyan strips on the engine fins for extra pop.

Now I need to settle on TypeScript typing for outline arrays and point helpers before writing the actual build code, making sure the types stay compatible without risky imports.

Still defining material colors...

Defining the joint hierarchy...

Still working out fork geometry...

Now I'm moving on to headlight, handlebars, fender, engine and frame details, then setting up the exhaust pipe as a swept path with a tapering radius function. I need to be careful with how the sweep callback provides frame data along the catmull path, and I'm assigning the taillight as a small sphere part.

Writing scaled geometry...

I'm positioning a license plate plane with a texture behind the fender, oriented along the z-axis, plus a small bracket rod connecting it to the frame.

Checking the remaining pieces: exhaust ring sweeps, final root return, lathe smoothing settings, engine fin colors, and fender arc sweeps. I'm also defining color sector ranges for the tank (navy, cream, orange) and starting the rear fender's sector layout.

I'm sketching the emblem SVG with a circle badge, chevron shape, and accent bar, then verifying the chevron coordinates line up cleanly before finalizing the lathe parameter types.

Now I'm placing the engine core components: positioning the crankcase center, cylinder base offsets front and rear, then adding fins, head boxes, and the navy valve cover along the cylinder axis direction.
